§ 21 · BasicsConstants, formalization and open problems

Explicit bad point sets

The proof is probabilistic: it shows that almost all random point sets are bad, but it cannot point to a specific one. Is there an explicit family of point sets with discrepancy Ω(log⁡3/2n)\Omega(\log^{3/2}n)Ω(log3/2n)? The paper names the main issue: how to retain the oscillation gained across many scales when the independent random digits are replaced by a deterministic choice.

Higher dimensions

For boxes in dimension d≥3d\ge3d≥3, it is known that Ωd(log⁡d−1n)≤Δd(n)≤Od(log⁡d−1/2n)\Omega_d(\log^{d-1}n)\le\Delta_d(n)\le O_d(\log^{d-1/2}n)Ωd​(logd−1n)≤Δd​(n)≤Od​(logd−1/2n); the gap is again log⁡n\sqrt{\log n}logn​. (The log⁡d+1/2n\log^{d+1/2}nlogd+1/2n of Section 7 is a weaker upper bound given by the factorization-norm method; Nikolov later improved it to log⁡d−1/2n\log^{d-1/2}nlogd−1/2n.) Bansal conjectured that the answer in ddd dimensions is O(log⁡d−1n)O(\log^{d-1}n)O(logd−1n); the theorem of the paper shows that this fails for d=2d=2d=2.

Which side is right in higher dimensions? Carry the calculation of Section 9 over to dimension ddd: the Brownian-sheet small-ball conjecture predicts the exponent ε−2log⁡2d−1(1/ε)\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{2d-1}(1/\varepsilon)ε−2log2d−1(1/ε), and balancing it against nln⁡2n\ln2nln2 gives log⁡d−1/2n\log^{d-1/2}nlogd−1/2n, which matches the known upper bound. The paper also stresses that this heuristic calculation does not transfer the conclusion to finite point sets. As for the proof, the argument of the paper uses two opposing resolutions, horizontal and vertical: when one coordinate is refined, the influence of a point is confined to a single vertical block (Section 15). An extension to higher dimensions needs an analogous local comparison when several coordinates are refined or coarsened at once.

Constants

As computed at the end of Section 18, the constant cAc_AcA​ given by the proof is extremely small: for A=12ln⁡2A=\frac12\ln2A=21​ln2 we get b=12451b=12451b=12451 and cA≈2−114.6c_A\approx2^{-114.6}cA​≈2−114.6, so the statement has real content only for astronomically large nnn. The paper says explicitly that it does not optimize cAc_AcA​.

Formalization and AI

The paper ends with an “AI methodology statement”. In brief: the author has been thinking about this problem since 2013; from July 2026 on, the author worked on it interactively with GPT and Claude, which first led to a proof based on a “killed suffix walk” and then to its simplification, the local-oscillation proof in Section 2 and the appendix of the paper; the same tools, together with Xean, were used to check the proof and to prepare the manuscript; there is a Lean formalization of the main lower-bound theorem, produced with GPT according to the paper; and the author verified the correctness and originality of all content. The code of the formalization is at github.com/wzskytop/tusnady-lean; for the tools used and the record of checks, the current description in that repository is authoritative. The paper is at arXiv:2610.08130.

The scope of the formalization should be kept clear. It covers the new lower bound of the paper: Theorem 1.1 for random points, and the deterministic lower bound that follows from it. The cited upper bound, the resulting statement Θ(log⁡3/2n)\Theta(\log^{3/2}n)Θ(log3/2n), the historical account, and the explanations and interactive figures added by this guide are outside its scope.

The repository's paper-to-code correspondence table maps the theorems and lemmas to their Lean declarations.

This guide adds derivations, examples and interactive figures. They are no substitute for formal verification, nor for independent review.

Other directions

In its discussion of related work, the paper mentions two directions. The first is online discrepancy: for points that arrive at random, earlier work studied online algorithms for intervals, stripes and Tusnády's problem. For uniform random arrivals in [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d, it is known that every online algorithm incurs discrepancy Ωd(log⁡d/2T)\Omega_d(\log^{d/2}T)Ωd​(logd/2T) within the first TTT arrivals, with constant probability (Bansal, Jiang, Singla and Sinha). Theorem 1.1 holds for every coloring, online or offline, so in the plane it raises this bound from log⁡T\log TlogT to log⁡3/2T\log^{3/2}Tlog3/2T. The second is data structures: discrepancy is related to lower bounds for range searching and approximate range counting, and the hard instances of the paper are random, so they may be useful for average-case lower bounds.

Check yourself · The whole guide

The gain per transition is n/M\sqrt{n/M}n/M​. Why not take nM\frac nMMn​ much larger than hhh?

The estimate of the gain holds for every nM\frac nMMn​. What is restricted is the estimate of the fluctuation: the total number hMhMhM of comparison rectangles must be at least of order nnn.

Which of the following is not a tool used in the proof?

The small-ball estimate for the Brownian sheet is used only to guess the scale (Section 9). The proof itself is entirely elementary.

In the plane, how much larger is combinatorial discrepancy than continuous discrepancy?

Continuous discrepancy is Θ(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n)Θ(logn), and combinatorial discrepancy is Θ(log⁡3/2n)\Theta(\log^{3/2}n)Θ(log3/2n). The extra factor is the square root gained at each level.
